ANTI-INFLATION BOARD REQUEST THAT BOARD BE ABOLISHED AND CREDITISTE PRINCIPLES APPLIED-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Considering that in spite of the government's anti-inflation measures, inflation continues to play havoc with the economy of every region of this country, especially in the food sector, considering also that the Anti-Inflation Board's decisions contribute to reducing the purchasing power of Canadian workers faced with soaring prices, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That this House consider the advisibility of abolishing the Anti-Inflation Board, which will cost more than $13 million in 1976 while jeopardizing the social peace of our country, and consider the implementation of measures proposed by the Social Credit as expounded in Bill C-328, An Act to provide for emergency measures to deal with the inflation of prices.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I request unanimous consent of the House to present a motion on an important and urgent matter.
Considering the very alarming unemployment increase in Quebec, particularly in the eastern area of the province, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That this House recommend to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion that at the time of the Ottawa-Quebec agreement, account should be taken of the disastrous economic conditions in the South Shore area, and that the economic needs of this area be mentioned in this agreement in order that the area might benefit from it and the number of its unemployed people be reduced.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN PRICE OF COPPER-GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO COUNTERACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct my question to the Minister of Finance. It arises out of recent reports that four major copper companies in Canada have raised their prices by about 5 per cent from 63 cents to 66 cents a pound. In view of the indications that the rise in price is the result of increases in the international price for copper rather than an increase in costs, and in light of the fact this increase in price is likely to work its way into the cost structure of the economy as a whole in coming weeks, what action does the minister intend to take immediately rather than wait for the Anti-Inflation Board to examine the quarterly reports of these companies which may take weeks or months, especially with the huge backlog facing the Anti-Inflation Board?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN PRICE OF COPPER-GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO COUNTERACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we indicated with respect to certain of the basic commodities, copper being the example, which trades, as it is said on a sawtooth market, that we were not applying the same criteria with regard to cost pass through that would apply with respect to other commodities. Indeed, 53 cents a pound was the price that had been prevailing for much of the early part of this year. Most of the copper in Canada was probably being sold at less than the cost of production. We should indeed look at the returns in the industry over a longer period and not apply strictly the cost pass-through formula. In that sense, the copper industry and other base metal industries would be treated in a different form than other companies in Canada with, however, the over-all restriction on profits that would apply, but over a longer period.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN PRICE OF COPPER-GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO COUNTERACT

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday I asked the acting minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board the following question which he took as notice, and I wonder if the minister can answer it for me today:
Many farmers are annoyed at the fact that in the 1974-75 crop year when they shipped cars of barley for malting, one car would be graded 2CW and the next No. 1 feed, yet both cars ended up for malting. speechtext:

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: USE OF X-RAY BY CHIROPRACTORS IN CANADA
speechtext:
1. The Radiation Protection Bureau of Health Protection Branch has recently initiated a computer program for collecting and analyzing data on the radiation doses received by Canadians in the course of medical and para-medical diagnostic procedures. Discussions are proceeding with provincial health departments at the technical level with the object of incorporating data from provincial X-ray surveillance programs into the central pool. However, the study has not yet proceeded to the point where the extent of use of X-rays by chiropractors can be evaluated. However, based upon utilization data of those provinces that pay for chiropractic and chiropractic X-rays under their medical care plans, and other related data, it is estimated that some 584,000 chiropractic X-rays were taken in Canada during 1974. As chiropractors are free to bill patients for additional services not covered by provincial plans, and since Workmen's Compensation Board cases were not included, the foregoing estimates likely understate the case. It appears that in practice, chiropractors generally do not use either total body or full spinal X-rays

as a matter of routine, but use X-rays for selected areas of the spinal column. Chiropractors use X-rays essentially for diagnostic purposes and not as a selective screening process or as a routine evaluation of new patients. The Health Protection Branch regards X-rays as an essential diagnostic tool, although their use involves some risk to the patient and should, therefore, be used only for valid medical reasons. Full spinal chiropractic X-ray examinations are not regarded by the Health Protection Branch as medically justifiable and this view is shared by the Canadian Medical Association.
2.	Based upon the utilization data and other factors mentioned in Part 1, it is estimated that some 144,000 services or 2.1 per cent of all chiropractic services rendred during 1974 were for children 14 years of age and under. Of these 144,000 services, 4.4 per cent involved the use of X-ray. When children 15 of 19 years of age are included, the number of services increases to 332,000 and the percentage of services involving the use X-ray increases to 5.2 per cent.
3.	The signature of a chiropractor is considered satisfactory for certification of federal employee sick leave (Form NHW-500). Subject to certain conditions chiropractic reports are accepted by the Department of National Health and Welfare medical officers who review Unemployment Insurance Commission medical assessments. Chiropractors are excluded from the list of passport guarantors. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police has added chiropractice as a benefit under its employee benefit plan. The Group Surgical Medical Insurance Plan for federal employees provides chiropractic benefits beyond those provided by the provincial insurance program. Several provincial health insurance plans cover chiropractic care on a limited basis, although the federal government does not share in these latter benefits as an insured service under the Medical Care Program. Workmen's Compensation Boards in all provinces except Quebec and Newfoundland have authorized workmen to receive chiropractic care.

speechtext: On the same point of order, Mr. Speaker, it is not the government's intention to have a long debate on second reading. Mr. Speaker, under the Financial
Administration Act, the government is requesting from the House, through this second bill, an appropriation of funds, the authorization to spend approximately $4,971 billion during the fiscal period 1976-77, which is slightly more than one quarter of the disbursements I submitted on February 18. By the same token, the government is asking for the authorization to borrow up to $6 billion to finance public works and other projects during the fiscal year starting April 1, an amount unchanged from 1975-76. It goes without saying that the government will not necessarily make use of this entire borrowing power. And my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has assured me that if such was the desire of the hon. members, he could personally come to a committee of the House to explain that borrowing policy for 1976-77.
As indicated yesterday by my colleague, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp), the changes made to procedure governing the passing of this bill give members the opportunity to express their opinion on the spending policy and the borrowing policy of the government.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I will take the opportunity offered me by this intervention on second reading to comment on and refute some of the criticisms directed toward this policy since the submission of the main estimates last February 18.
Hon. members are aware that many Canadians are concerned about the scope and effectiveness of public spending at all levels of government. We share these concerns which have been promoted by the abnormally high increase in federal and provincial expenditures during the last two years. Accordingly, we have taken a series of measures to limit the growth of expenditures, to curb the expansion of the public service and to improve productivity throughout the government.
Costs can be, and have been controlled; productivity gains can be, and have been, achieved in the federal public service. This is very much the business of the Treasury Board and its secretariat, and they have been far from inactive. Ministers and senior executives will testify-even complain, occasionally-that over the years the budgetary controls administered by the secretariat's program branch have become much more rigorous. The administrative policy branch has kept regulations and guidelines constantly under review and tightened them whenever feasible and justifiable.
The personnel policy branch had managed to keep the salaries and wages of federal public servants at levels

comparable to the average remuneration of other Canadians in similar occupational categories. The planning branch, apart from conducting, each year, effectiveness and efficiency analyses in major policy areas, as well as government-wide managerial studies, has developed and begun to implement systems of operational performance measurements and methods of benefit-cost analysis applicable to government operations.

Judging from the accusations they make right and left, it is not unwarranted to remind hon. members of the opposition some of our recent initiatives in this field.
On January 22 of this year, a Treasury Board circular informed federal departments and agencies of reductions they have to make in administrative practices of the government, to comply with the Prime Minister's undertaking to reduce government spendings, as part of the fight against inflation. These reductions affect in particular the purchase of photocopying equipment and of motor vehicles, the participation of public servants in non-government conferences, office furniture, travels and the use of taxis.
I do not believe these measures will enable us to save huge amounts. However they will generate necessary restraint in the public administration and put an end to abuses which, though not too frequent, rightly concerned Canadian taxpayers.
In February, I urged the Treasury Board officials, in the memoranda they were sending to deputy ministers and managers of federal agencies, to remind them of the announcement made last December by the Prime Minister, who emphasized that the budgetary restraint policy of the government was not to be applied in the current year only, but had to be maintained for several years in order to be efficient.
In early March, following the review by the Auditor General on financial management and control within the federal government, I announced the creation of a new branch of the financial administration within the secretariat of the Treasury Board. On the same day, I announced to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts that we fully agreed with 22 out of 34 recommendations by the Auditor General, that we accepted with some reservations 10 other recommendations and that only two were unacceptable to us. It has been argued by some people, when hearing of this new branch, that the government had finally decided to appoint a "watchdog" for federal spendings. It is not so, Mr. Speaker. As I said earlier, the Program Branch of the secretariat has been examining the estimates of the various departments for a long time, just as the Planning Branch has been assessing their efficiency and output and the Administrative Policy Branch has been reviewing their practices in many areas, including financial administration. The re-structure now under way is rather designed to strengthen and tighten financial controls that have existed for many decades.

To complete this review of some of our recent initiatives toward better spending control, I might add that the secretary of the Treasury Board, at my request, tabled this morning in the public accounts committee the new benefit-cost analysis guide which is being issued to all depart-
March 25, 1976

ments and agencies. As you know, the Treasury Board has been actively involved in fostering the use of this modern management technique by individual government departments, while carrying out itself a number of benefit-cost studies of major expenditure programs.
Put simply, benefit-cost analyses can provide ministers and public administrators with some rough and ready measures of the social usefulness of a project or program by considering all the benefits to society arising from it- even the less tangible one-and comparing them with the total cost of the project. It is not a substitute for administrative, common sense or political judgment, but it provides a more concrete basis, more economic facts, on which to apply such common sense or judgment. The new guide prepared by the planning branch of the Treasury Board secretariat lays down the conceptual framework for benefit-cost analysis, discusses the methodological problems which government analysts must resolve, and gives them practical advice on how they should proceed.
Finally, I would like to announce a further measure to trim down operating costs and raise productivity levels within the federal public service. At my request, the Secretary of the Treasury Board wrote last week to all deputy ministers and heads of agencies to inform them of the government's decision to establish a senior interdepartmental committee on administrative improvements. The terms of reference of the committee are as follows: first, to identify those areas in which improvements can be made in the management and control of administrative inputs; second, to establish priorities for the review of those areas; third, to establish or redefine the study objective and the organization required to develop solutions to each of the identified areas in which improvements can be made; fourth, to make recommendations to the cabinet, as required, through the Treasury Board, on the administrative improvements proposed as a result of the studies; fifth, to recommend to the Treasury Board the most effective means of implementing and monitoring the administrative improvements approved by cabinet as a result of the studies; sixth, to report semi-annually to the Treasury Board and, if appropriate, to the cabinet on the progress of the committee.
A number of departments and agencies will be permanently involved in the committee because the scope and complexity of their operations require attention on a continuing basis; others will be invited to participate whenever the committee deems it useful to review operations under their responsibility where efficiency could be improved and savings made. But I suspect that this is far too complicated to discuss in detail in the House with hon. members of the opposition. They are not really interested in a more efficient public service or in more effective government programs. What they want is blood on, the floor and a knife in the financial gut of every department, even if its operations are vital to the Canadian economy; even if thousands of people are thrown out of work, and even if economic and social progress is brought to a halt.

The expenditure policy of the government between 1968 and 1973 can be considered as the continuation of post-war Liberal economics which have been so beneficial for Canada. Federal expenditures were allowed to grow at a rate which varied from year to year depending upon the needs of federal programs and the requirements of the economy as a whole. Because we introduced new programs and expanded many of the existing ones, the share of national output, absorbed by federal expenditures, increased slightly-by less than 1 per cent on average, but the growth of real GNP remained above 5 per cent during that entire five-year period, with the single exception of 1970. Moreover, the surpluses accumulated during the good years, on a national accounts basis, more than offset the deficit incurred in 1971 and 1972. What happened, then, in the past two years? Why were we not, in 1974 and 1975, able to maintain the balanced policy of the previous five years? Why has the increase in federal expenditures been higher than usual? Why was it necessary to absorb a sizeable deficit last year?
My colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), will have much to say on these questions in his forthcoming budget speech. However, the short answer is that the four-fold increase in oil prices, compounding years of chronic inflation and instability in international markets, plunged the world economy into its worst slump since the end of the Second World War-and, confronted with declining exports and sluggish domestic demand, our government simply rejected the Bennett solution. We refused to make matters worse by savage cuts in federal spending, even when slower growth cut into our revenues and when inflation bloated our expenditures.

With the support of all provincial governments, including those of oil producing provinces, we refused to let the oil importing provinces of eastern Canada bear, without relief, the full burden of higher energy prices. But that cost a great deal of money. Had it not been for oil compensation payments, the over-all increase of federal expenditures- measured on the public accounts basis-would have been about $4.2 billion less in the last two fiscal years as well as the one beginning on April 1, but the private sector would then have been saddled with a huge financial burden which would have depressed the economy even more. The fact that the recession was relatively milder in Canada than in most other industrial countries, and much milder than in the United States, bears testimony to the basic soundness of our economic policies. We have managed to avoid a contraction in real output even in 1975, a year when only half a dozen members of the OECD group were able to achieve any real growth.
In conclusion, I should like to remind our critics that the main estimates of expenditure are only one half of the government's budgetary policy. They must wait for the budget speech proper to learn about the other half, namely, the government's policy and expectations concerning revenues, borrowings and general economic conditions during 1976 and the early part of 1977. I am sure my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) will greatly enlighten them on that issue.
Unlike Conservatives and New Democrats, Liberals are not dogmatic about public expenditures. We believe that the government should not hesitate to spend more when the state of the economy and the general welfare of Canadians require it. But we also believe that the government should not hesitate to trim its sails when conditions change and the private sector provides adequate impetus for economic growth. In addition, whatever may be the level of expenditures, the government constantly tries to ensure that funds are spent efficiently and that Canadians are provided with effective public services-and I mean all ministers, not just the President of the Treasury Board. I am so enthusiastic about my job that I sometimes get carried away.

I am glad he changed his tune somewhere after the middle part of his speech, because I had assumed that this procedure, which was a special procedure, was brought about because of the absolutely ridiculous ways in which this parliament, representing as we do the people of the country, is without the ability realistically to review the estimates and expenditures of government.
A few minutes ago the minister suggested that standing committees can review estimates. I tell the minister that I and other hon. members, including government supporters, have attempted to do this elsewhere, and I tell him that our rules of procedure do not permit us to examine in depth the details of government spending.
Many years ago, when I was a student at Carleton University, I used to sit in the gallery and watch the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and others consider the estimates in committee of the whole. Then the House exercised control over government spending. We watched committee of the whole deal with the estimates of each minister. The consideration of estimates was not restricted by time. The quality of ministers' answers determined how long estimates were given consideration. Only after the minister had answered all questions were the estimates passed. Some ministers were candid with the committee, others were not so candid. When ministers were candid, no matter how complex their estimates were, the estimates were passed. If ministers did not answer fully, or refused to answer, or evaded questions-as ministers have been known to do from time to time-the estimates were held up.
The rules were changed in 1969. The review of estimates was made the responsibility of standing committees and the rights of members restricted. It became difficult for members to determine the real cost and purpose of various provisions in the estimates, and almost impossible to see if they were sound. It is one thing for any minister to tell the House he has embarked on a program, but quite another for parliament to be satisfied that the program is operating properly as the minister may claim. At present, the representatives of this country's 23 million people are given little right to examine the estimates. Certain things, nonetheless, are apparent. The government claims that it has no control over the growth of certain expenditures, but it is evident that it is responsible for increased spending in certain areas in which there is no evidence of diminution of costs.
Let me quote some figures. About 45 per cent of the increase in government spending is attributable to grants, contributions and transfer payments. Yet in other areas, significant savings could be made. It is clearly evident that the bulk of the increase in spending is accounted for by spending in areas where the government exercises a high degree of control. Consider the following categories of increases: salaries and wages have increased 13.6 per cent; other personnel costs, 18.4 per cent; transport and communications, 12.4 per cent; information, 16.5 per cent; professional and special services, 9.9 per cent; rentals, 18 per cent; purchased repair and upkeep, 15.1 per cent; utilities, material and supplies, 13.5 per cent; capital, land, building and equipment, 11.9 per cent; capital, machinery

and equipment, 24.4 per cent; public debt charges, 23.1 per cent; and all other expenditures, 36.4 per cent.
Clearly, the minister's claim that the government is exercising restraint is unfounded. The facts are to the contrary. Members of the government talk a great deal about fighting inflation and about the white paper on inflation, but the government does not intend to follow its own guidelines when increasing wages, salaries and other personnel costs. I suggest that an examination of the estimates will show I am right. If the government is sincere in what it says about restraint, let it practice that restraint. It alone must decide if it will follow its own policy. It cannot look to the opposition for guidance; it must look to itself. It alone can determine if it will follow its own policy. The government is basically responsible for establishing shortterm as well as long-term priorities for expenditures, and it has not done so. For instance-

Mr. Chairman, I respect that. Questions will be asked. The difficulty is that the minister is most reluctant to answer questions asked in committee of the whole or elsewhere. I was talking about the government's restraint program and spending priorities. What has happened? Ministers are beating their breasts, telling us they practice restraint. But what, actually, are they doing? In these times of restraint, the government has launched a program for decentralizing government. The cost is not less than between $50,000 and $60,000 per employee involved. Is that restraint? How much is the government spending on information? According to my information, the total cost of information services and staff is at least $138 million. If we make reasonable allowance for the cost of accommodation and support services, that figure rises to about $150 million.
What do we have? What do we get for it? Does anybody feel well informed? Government press hand-outs are considered by the press as a bad joke in terms of number and quality-glossy publications, overproduced, underread and poorly created. What has the over $5 million budget of
March 25, 1976

external affairs done to our image abroad? What will the planned increase of over $1 million in 1976-77 add? There is the first question.
The $14 million spent by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce will be increased by over $4.5 million in 1976-77. While tourism seems to be doing well with its $834 million, what is the other $10 million going to do for us? It, visibly, has not done much for our exports recently. Why does Statistics Canada need almost $4 million more in 1976-77? What does the $10 million, plus, spending by national defence do to improve our defence posture when we have not even made up our mind which way we are going? These are the matters to which this government should direct itself-and not in terms of its restraint program, a program that, as a matter of fact, is not a restraint program at all.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
There is one other matter which affects every member of the House of Commons. It is the ability that we, as parliamentarians-not just ministers or government supporters, but all of us- have to examine expenditures of government. What is the attitude of a bureaucrat toward committees of the House of Commons? I have a quote from a retired bureaucrat, Frank Howard. He was a communications officer, and is now a writer. He tells us what he thinks of the parliamentary system and the ability of committees to find out how the Queen's money, the money of the people of this country, is spent. This is what he had to say about his job as a communications officer, and I quote from the March 7 edition of Saturday Night:
I came to worry about what I was doing to the press. My job was to manipulate it. The simple truth was that it was easy: the press didn't know how to ask the right questions, so you went out and fed them the answers you wanted.
With parliament we operated the same way. We figured out a way of getting off easy with Commons committees. At the first opportunity possible we'd get the top scientist in the department to speak. He'd come across with a whole lot of stuff about gigahertzes and geostationary orbits and if some MP asked a question, he'd say no, they hadn't quite understood and come back with more jargon, and so the MP would give up and none of them would come even close to understanding the real problems of communications.
Here is what he had to say about the right of parliamentarians to know:
In the end, you come to view information as something you put out when it's to your advantage. By your advantage, I mean the advantage of the system. People within the system who don't understand that information is a commodity, to be used and exploited for the system's advantage, don't get along.
Parliament can't control government. MPs don't know what questions to ask, and even if they asked them, there's no way of forcing the government to give answers. Even ministers don't control the bureaucracy. Ministers spend their first year trying to get into their department, and then they're co-opted by the department. For people outside trying to represent the public interest, it's even worse. Ranged up against them is a bureaucracy that amounts to a vast information processing machine with years and years of experience.
That says something to every member of parliament. It says something to those who want to see the rules reformed. The government is always talking about shortening the length of debate. The government House leader talks about television in the House. There are much more important things to be done. Forget about the cosmetics.

Give us the tools. Give us the means to ask the proper questions. Give us the answers to our questions. Make our committees independent. Give us those tools and we will show this or any other government what ought to be within the power of a parliament, properly equipped, to inquire. We would not use these tools to obstruct, as we are accused of doing, but honestly and objectively to look at the estimates of each department. We do not have that power, and that is what we require.
When the government House leader raises in this House the necessity of reforming the rules, I completely agree with him. However, I want the government House leader to understand that if we are going-
Do you want a soap-box?

speechtext: Apparently the hon. member does not care if the regulations are changed. If we are going to make the legislative machinery move more quickly, the price for that change is going to be a heavy one indeed. The price will be to give to parliament assembled here and in the various committees a revision of the committees' system so there can, at long last, be something that we have not had since the rule changes were pushed through this parliament by closure in the sixties; that is, the right to know and the right to examine.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have something to say about asking questions. The man who wrote the article I quoted had the following to say about that matter:
The people who are interested in finding out things have to be given the means of finding things out. There's a rough rule of thumb in government that you spend about two to three per cent of the budget of a program on information relating to the program. Why not insist that, say, one-tenth of one per cent of a program's budget be channelled into research by the opposition parties. If you put down $80 million for LIP this year, then you put down $80,000 for research into LIP. And so on. Now if you started that tomorrow, the opposition wouldn't know what to do; they'd still concentrate on the horror stories. But over time, they'd build a competent research staff. This might turn into a bureaucracy. At least it would be a counter-bureaucracy.
If these suggestions were taken, we would see, for the first time in many years, an honest examination of government expenditures. It would not only serve parliament, which it should serve first, but the government as well. The government would know that committees were a well-informed, articulate sounding board for their programs. After the programs were considered by the committees, they would be acceptable without suspicion-and this is something that is very important. The knowledge that we have, in terms of the operation of government, is vested in the bureaucracy, the government. In terms of parliament and its operation, access to knowledge has become overweighted on the government side.
I ask the President of the Treasury Board, as the keeper of the public purse, whether he is prepared to recommend to his ministry, as a first priority in terms of spending, and to the commissioners of internal economy of this place-of which he is one-a substantial increase, on a negotiated basis, with respect to funds for the operation of research offices of all political parties represented in this House.

I make this request so that the work of this parliament can determine the examination of the estimates, the study of the government's legislative program, the study of its priorities, the questioning of its objectives, finding out whether those objectives are being met, and discussing whether the offices, in terms of cost analysis, cost-benefit work referred to by the minister, are being carried out. We in this parliament should be able to examine that work. You are an officer of parliament, Mr. Chairman, and you must care about it as well. If this kind of thing does not start now, we will see a continuation of the ability of the government to stonewall not only in this chamber but in the committee. Those things which should be exposed will not be exposed, and as to those things for which the government ought to get credit, we will not know about them in a way in which we can honestly accept them. If this is done, this institution will take on a new life of its own. I hope the minister will consider the propriety, the rightness of asking for an amendment to the rules of this House so that we can bring back, once more at least, some departmental estimates into the committee of the whole in the old way.
Some people look upon this public institution with some cynicism. From what we have seen in the last few days, I can understand that. But what I suggest would constitute a great improvement.

Mr. Chairman, like the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, we welcome this day during which we can spend some time on the estimates for the year just ahead of us. We shall all discover very soon that the day will go very fast, and my contribution to avoiding that will be to speak for less than the 20 minutes I am allowed.
I was interested in the reference the previous speaker made to the days when he sat in the gallery as a student watching some of us who were already on the floor dealing with estimates in the committee of supply. I was a member of the committee which changed all that and put the estimates into the various committees. We were involved in quite a struggle when that was done in 1968, but I am prepared to say that we did win certain gains though we also suffered a very real loss. I think we had very much more control when the estimates were on the floor and there was no time limit. I know we cannot go back to that system. The number of departments, the amount of money which is spent, the items on which the money is spent-all these things have multiplied so much that we cannot go back to that earlier arrangement. However, I think that when we reform the rules with respect to the handling of expenditures we ought to make provision for bringing back to the floor of the House of Commons two or three departments a year, picked by the opposition, and discussion on those estimates when they are on the floor should be without time limit. If it is done the other way, ministers can just sit it out, members on the government side can exercise their right to use up some of the time, and any sense of control by the House of Commons over expenditure of money is gone. However, I do not want to be guilty of using this day, when we have estimates before us, in discussing procedure, though I welcome the comments the

hon. member for Grenville-Carleton made in that direction.
I welcome the speech made by the President of the Treasury Board. I enjoy him when he deals with the technicalities of his position. I enjoy him just as much, perhaps more, when he launches into a political tirade. He is good at it. I have seen him grow into quite a politician since he first came here some 14 years ago. But I want to say to him there is one taunt he may think he can throw at the Progressive Conservative party but he cannot throw it at us. He likes to say to the Progressive Conservatives that though they call for restraint, though they call for cuts in expenditure, they also demand new expenditures. He knows he cannot throw that charge at us because we have said many times that we realize that civilization costs money. He knows that we do not look upon government taxing and spending as a form of highway robbery but as a means of redistributing the wealth which is created in this country.
Our quarrel with the government is not with its level of spending but with its order of priorities. Right now, if the government wants to talk about restraint, about cutting expenditures, the way to implement such a program is not just to cut everything by a certain percentage, not for the President of the Treasury Board to become "Mr. No" to every one of his colleagues, but to make cuts where they can be applied without causing suffering, and to realize that in some cases the circumstances call for increases.
We have before us today an interim supply bill which provides for three-twelfths of all the estimates for 1975-76 and some more twelfths for certain of the departments. This being so, discussion can cover virtually an unlimited range of subjects. We regret very much that the estimates are such that they carry out the government's announced intention to freeze family allowances at the 1975 level. Even in a period of restraint, even when cuts are being made, it is the responsibility of the government to face up to the difficulties of those who are in need, and we contend that failure to escalate family allowances in 1976 in accordance with the rise in the cost of living is a gross piece of unfairness.
By the same token, I regret that no provision is made in the main estimates for an increase in the basic amount of old age security payments. Provision is there for an escalation corresponding to the rise in the cost of living, and this applies not only to the basic amount but to the guaranteed income supplement. However, the government takes the view that nothing more needs to be done in connection with that issue, and says-especially to hon. members on my right, "If you want expenditures cut, you cannot be asking for further expenditures at the same time." I say, again, that what concerns us is the scale of priorities, how the money is spent.
I cannot join in all the complaints the previous speaker made about government spending, but I suggest to the President of the Treasury Board that there is cause for complaint when the number of public servants in the SX category has risen from 400 a few years ago to over 1,000. I would remind the minister that between 1969 and 1974, while he was minister of Indian affairs and northern development, the number of public servants in that category in his department-these are the highest paid public serv-

ants-rose from 16 to 47. This is hardly restraint: it is a sample of what the government does.
Then there are these huge expenses on buildings for the defence department, some of which may not be necessary; and there is the kind of expenditure we seem to be facing in connection with the Lockheed contract or agreement. The people of Canada wonder what is going on, and have reason to be cynical. Our position as a party is not that the government is doing the wrong thing in raising money by taxation and in spending it. Our contention is that the money is being spent, in many cases, on the wrong things-and that where money is needed, this government does not come through. We think it is wrong for the President of the Treasury Board simply to stand up with confidence, because he is saying "No" to everybody else, and say "No" to those on family allowances, those on old age pensions, and so on.
Initially I said I would try not to use the 20 minutes that is allotted to each of us because I hoped that during the day a number of members could take part. Some of my colleagues have specific points they want to speak about, and since I probably will not get a chance to speak again in the day, I should like to say now that I welcome the fact that the Minister of Finance is going to come in to deal with the borrowing business. I will not go into the technicalities of that, but I hope when he comes he will answer some questions in relation to the "Orion" which Lockheed is trying to sell us. My colleague, the hon. member for Greenwood, was asking questions about this "Orion" business today. We welcome this day and we want more days like it, but we do not want days that end the way this one will, with the clock telling us it is 9.45 p.m. and we have to quit. This year however, 130,000 public servants are renegotiating their collective agreements with the federal government. Earlier the House leader for the New Democratic Party-
He spoke about the increases in the government. Of course there was a great increase in some departments.
All departments.

Tell us what you did when you were minister of Indian affairs.

We increased expenditures in Indian affairs when I was there, and I am not ashamed of that. It is true that I spent a lot of money when I was minister of Indian affairs, but we had a very difficult situation. For the first time in our history, this nation gave money to the Indians in order to help them get organized. I was somewhat interested in the minister's comments with regard to giving the Indians money "to give him hell". I think he would be better off if he gave them money to enable them to have a decent living in this country. But this is not the area to which I want to dedicate most of my comments. I wish to touch on a subject of great importance which, according to the government, does not have too much political sex appeal. I refer to the subject of medical research. It seems to me that the attitude of the President of the Treasury Board to this subject has been inexcusable insofar as his policies may result in the decimation of the research community in this country.
I do not wish to sound as if I am speaking contrary to what other members have been saying, which is that as a whole the minister and the government have failed to make cuts in expenditures. As a general rule, that is true: they have not made the required cuts in government spending in keeping with the times in which we live. However, the research field is a strange place in which to have cuts. Cuts in expenditures in respect of research are, indeed, not cuts at all, but the fact. The minister is getting a little excited. I wish he would pay attention to what is being said. He has intervened to say there were not any cuts. The fact is that the budget has been frozen. Since inflation has been very rampant in this country, and in so far as medical research is concerned it has been running somewhere in the vicinity of 18 per cent, when the budget is frozen in the face of 18 per cent inflation this is the same as cutting it by 18 per cent in practical terms.
What we are seeing here is a government which is trying to ride to political glory on the back of the research community of this country. This is just as shameful as riding to glory on the back of the poor, which the minister has been doing by putting a freeze on family allowances and thereby making things difficult for the children and mothers of our nation. The minister has challenged our party to say where he should be making cuts where he has not done so. I could give him a long list. One place is in respect of the Canada Development Corporation. That could be cut out completely. The other is Petro-Can. It is unnecessary. Then there is the Prime Minister's office and the Privy Council office. The extravagant expenditures by the government are completely unnecessary, but nothing is being done about that.
Then we come to something closer to the minister's heart. How about the bilingual program? How necessary is that in so far as our social and economic structure is concerned at a time of restraint? We know that the bilingual program not only has failed in unifying Canada but has divided Canada very substantially. What this boils down to is that the minister is saying to the people of Canada that he does not mind if they die of a heart attack so long as on their death-bed they can speak in both official languages.
Nonsense.

That is the kind of priority we are being faced with. The minister does not like to hear these facts, but the fact is that if he would look at the total budget of the bilingual program he would see that there is a somewhat mixed-up priority on his part, and not on my part.

Does the minister say that is a good objective, or does he say that it should be cut?
There is no cut.

I would like to conclude by stating the objectives of medical research. The second objective was to improve the application of scientific principles to health care. I do not think anybody can argue with that. It is a good objective, and it should be upheld. The third objective is to ensure an adequate research base for education in the health sciences. I think that is the area which is being severely damaged by the short-sightedness of this minister. The fourth one is to support the training of research investigators in the health sciences. That follows the broad field of education. We are not training our research investigators any longer, and we are asking them to go into other fields of employment because there are no funds in this field. The final objective is to support research contributing to new knowledge in the health sciences. I know that the attitude of this government was that it did not want to be confused by knowledge and facts. Perhaps that is why we are faced with these cuts.
Excuse me, Mr. Chairman. Just for clarification, may I give some information to the hon. member?

speechtext: Thin skin, eh?
It is a fact.
The minister's skin is thin.
Don't ask me questions if you don't want my answers.

I hope the minister has a pen and will take note of all the questions and answer them all at once. I have many questions to ask, and perhaps it would be easier if he would simply answer them later. I want to compare the renewal rate for April, 1976, of 60 per cent with that of last November when it was 75 per cent. So the minister can see the difference. Last November, 25 per cent of the projects were thrown out; but in April, 40 per cent of ongoing projects will be cut.
In terms of new applications-and research is not simply intended to carry on programs which were started, two, three or ten years ago-if we want to satisfy one of the objectives to which I have referred, that is, to contribute 
new information in the research field, we must also accept new applications for entirely new programs. Starting in April, 345 such applications were filed, of which only 10 per cent were accepted, or only some 35. That means that the other 300 were simply turned away. If the minister is pleased and proud of that kind of record, let him rise in the House and say so. If I were in his boots, I would be ashamed of such a record. The argument which he has used from time to time has been that this is going to save money.
Let us look at the people who are in research. I am inclined to think that a significant number of them, perhaps 30 per cent or 50 per cent, are medical doctors. I do not have the exact figures, but I am sure the minister will be able to find them. Once these people are rejected, in terms of applications to do research, they will not go and dig ditches, drive a truck, go on welfare or on unemployment insurance, which the minister perhaps would like them to do: those medical doctors will go into practice. We know that a busy physician in active practice not only draws a salary above that of a researcher in a health insurance program footed by provincial and federal governments, but generates substantially higher costs in terms of expenditures in hospitals, laboratories, X-ray departments, and so on. Indeed, it has been estimated that an active, practising physician generates a total cost of perhaps a quarter of a million dollars.
So we may be rejecting a research project which may cost $50,000 a year, if we say, roughly, that a researcher's salary is $20,000 a year and he may require another $30,000 for equipment, staff, and so on. Even from the short-term point of view, there is no saving at all. In fact, it will create a higher cost to the taxpayer than if this budget had not been cut and these people were kept in the research field. I do not believe, either from the short-term point of view or the long-term point of view, that cutting costs in medical research will in any way save money to the taxpayer.
The minister became a little excited when I said he was cutting costs. I have here the newsletter to which I made reference previously. It indicates a substantial number of things which have been cut from the usual program and have been followed by the Medical Research Council. The first one was the cut respecting the planned heart research project. I thought it was rather strange and ironical to see the Minister of National Health and Welfare, on television a week or two ago, doing the three-step test to check his cardiac fitness while at the same time he cancelled the heart research program which had been planned by the Medical Research Council.
Shame!

It is typical of the kind of priorities by which this government lives. I think we, as a people, as a country, and a parliament, should have some explanation for this ridiculous state of affairs. Just to get back to the cuts, the Medical Research Council "Newsletter," volume 6, No. 2, of January 15, 1976, indicates that for the fiscal year 1976-77 the programs of the Medical Research Council are altered as follows: no visiting scientists awards will be made for the coming year; no funds for summer undergraduate research scholarships will be made available to the deans of the medical, dental and pharmaceutical facul-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I want to reply to some of the points made at the beginning of this debate by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, who I regret is not in the House at the moment, and by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Walter will be right back. You can go ahead with Stanley.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: At the beginning of every debate of this nature there is an almost routine reference to the good old days. The allegation is made in the days of committee of supply, parliament did some great and wonderful things, and that this place has somehow degenerated into an institution which has no control whatever over estimates any more.
That is right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
I sat in a parliament which was alleged to have been so great-and so did you, Mr. Chairman, as I think back-and I recall what happened in the parliament of 1963-1965 in which I served. It is true that the estimates procedure was in committee of supply and committee of the whole House, and hon. members who sat on the other side eventually had to face their own consciences. I know the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was one who did. It was not an examination of estimates, it was a procedure of obstruction which took place, and I remember
Interim Supply
very clearly that over 20 days were used on a very small item of supplementary estimates involving a single department. It was passed eventually without even a dollar being changed, and that was alleged to have been the great democratic procedure of the House of Commons in those days.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: All the members of this House came to the conclusion that parliament was being disgraced by the procedure, and that it was not what it was alleged to be by those on the other side who spoke. They realized that the people who voted us to this place expected us to do a job and not to go through the kind of sham which took place in committee of the whole. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was attempting to say things in, I think, a fair and impartial way. He said that when the changes of 1968 were introduced, from his point of view there were certain gains and certain losses. He admitted that there were improvements, and the strengthening of the committee system is, I am sure, one of them. The attempt to deal in a more fundamental and honest way with the question of estimates has probably plagued more than just this parliament. The British parliament has grappled with this question, and if I may suggest, with even less success than this parliament.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
On an inventory of gains, I wish that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had catalogued a few more of the gains which actually did develop, because there were very definitely some. One of the gains which did not come right away, but which came a little later, as referred to by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, was the development of research services in this House of Commons. Research services were made available to every party. It is for hon. members of the parties to answer for the use made of these research services. If they are used well, this House is a better place: if they are used poorly, this House is not doing its job.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton said the remedy was to give more and more money. I have been trying to find out just what would be an appropriate sum. His answer is that of the old Samuel Gompers and the American Federation of Labour, just give us more and more. He does not quantify what he wants; he does not offer any standards; he just says we have to have more. In one breath he says, "don't spend as much," and in the next breath he says, "Give us more research services." In fairness, we have to come to some understanding of the goals and objectives of the elected representatives and parties in this House and how they are going to deal with the problem.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Just remember, you may be in opposition some day.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: No doubt. I hope to see more than one change in government before I am through. I hope I will be able to survive as long as my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, although that would be a very long time indeed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: Let us look again at what has to be done by way of innovations in an attempt to come to grips with the problem. Just about a year ago a package of new rules was introduced into this House, and I think everyone agreed that the rules introduced were steps forward; for example, the termination of the question period at three o'clock, the reduction of the number of Standing Order 43 motions which could be introduced, and so on. However, I wonder how many hon. members opposite recall that one of the items in the package which was offered was the ability to call departments before the House, in committee of the whole, on supply days. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is looking at me, and I am sure he remembers that. It was part of the package and there were hon. members on this side of the House who looked on this with some trepidation. They were concerned that this was giving a great deal. But I must say that the one or two rather feeble attempts to use that particular item in this House were not very impressive. Hon. members in the House gave up even trying.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre intervenes, but he was one who not long ago said in the House that he hoped to bring individual ministers and individual departments back into committee of the whole again so that there could be some control over them. I think that is almost a complete paraphrasing of his words. When the opportunity was offered in the rules' package of a year ago, I suggest that no good use was made of that opportunity by hon. members opposite.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Virtue does not reside just on any one side. We are all members! We all carry out our responsibility and we are all aware of the problems of estimates. There is too much money, government is too big and it is hard to come to grips with it. The amount of knowledge which individual members can assimilate and use effectively is limited. We are aware of this, so there is a real attempt being made today by the Auditor General before the public accounts committee. It was looking at the estimates book, looking at the procedures, looking at the changes made as a result of an investigation by an outside group which examined the question of estimates some years ago and offered suggestions for reform. There is an honest difference of opinion amongst representatives of the Treasury Board who have maintained with a good deal of conviction before the committee that the new form of estimates is an improvement. A group of independent accountants was brought in by the Auditor General; they made the argument that the changes were not an improvement and tried to suggest a better format.
Hon. members opposite said that we were not doing the right things on estimates. It is like a ritual, Mr. Chairman: they have an obligation to go to the public accounts committee, make representations to the Auditor General, tell him how the estimates can be improved and make suggestions for improvement in the means by which hon. mem-

bers of this House can exercise their ancient and democratic right of voting supply.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
It is not enough just to bitch about it, to just say time after time that parliament has lost something, that in the good old days we did great things and that now we are a sad reflection of what we were before; that is not the way to deal with the question. Some very good and diligent members from the other side sit on the public accounts committee. There is a definite lack of partisan atmosphere in the examination by the public accounts committee, and I think it is to the credit of hon. members on all sides to recognize that we have a problem.
I have just made these observations because I hoped that when the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, for whom I have the greatest personal respect-he represents a riding adjoining mine, and we have known each other for 20 years-would do more than talk about the good old days, the great things that were done and our democratic right. He referred to articles by a former member of the public service, Mr. Frank Howard. Mr. Chairman, I served nine years in the public service and appeared before committees to answer questions for my minister. I had to go through the whole exercise, and I cannot share the view that this parliament has in any way lost any of its democratic rights.
There are just one or two other things I should like to add. I listened to the hon. member for Athabasca and I should like to set the record straitht on some of the things he said. He repeated allegations of cuts to the Medical Research Council. Mr. Chairman, I am informed that the actual money voted for medical research in the fiscal year 1974-75 was $42,800,000, in the fiscal year 1975-76 it was $47,400,000, in the fiscal year 1976-77 the amount indicated in the estimates is $48,400,000.
I know there are hon. members an all sides of the House on the public accounts committee who are more competent than I am to review the heroic efforts of the Auditor General to come to grips with the basic problem of how an elected legislature should deal with estimates of the magnitude on which we have to vote. I hope they will intervene in this debate.

Mr. Chairman, my time is limited and I want to spend most of it dealing with the question of medical research. Let us get the record clear when this minister, who has designated himself "Mr. No", boasts so loudly. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre put some of the figures on the record in so far as we have them. It is not always easy for us to get answers. If a member of parliament does not ask precisely the right question-and it is difficult to know all the titles and categories-he gets an answer only to the question he asks.
Sometimes, not even that.

There is one small, but important group that I am concerned about-the senior executive officers, the people who earn from $30,000 to $66,000 a year. According to the figures supplied by the minister's department, in 1968 there were 381 of these people; by 1974 there were

1,062. I will leave it to the minister to calculate the percentage increase. In the Treasury Board alone, the increase was from 20 to 47. So when the minister says he is "Mr. No", he is "Mr. No" with a good deal of reservation. I think he knows he is being unfair when he critizes us or suggests that we object to the increased expenditures on the native people of this country. What we object to is the tremendous increase in the amount of money that has gone to senior bureaucrats.
I am not going to take much time to expound on this theme, but I suggest to the minister and to the parliamentary secretary that if they are honest and want to look at the situation realistically, they should look at the current issue of Saturday Night which contains an article by Douglas Hartle who for some time was a deputy secretary of the Treasury Board. I think Mr. Hartle knows what he is talking about, and his article shows how far out of whack the system is. As the hon. member for Athabasca was talking about the plight of medical research, one might have thought it a figment of the imagination of the opposition. We heard the usual rude and loud interjection of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. If she could read- which I sometimes doubt-I would suggest that she should take advantage-
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order-
Order, please. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, on a point of order.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to suggest to the hon. member that not only can I read, but I have written and I have achieved a certain degree of success, where the hon. member seems to have failed. Mr. Chairman, I know the hon. member: she interjects, and hon. members on this side know how often she interjects. I want to put a few things on the record so there will be no misunderstanding of what people in the scientific community have to say about the fact that the government has frozen the amount of money given to medical research in the current fiscal year. I should like to read from a letter sent out by Dr. Malcolm Brown, chairman of the Medical Research Council of Canada, a government agency. The letter is dated January 16, 1976, and is addressed to the deans of the medical colleges in this country. It reads in part:
The visiting scientist, research professorships and summer undergraduate research scholarships programs have been suspended for 1976-77.
The June, 1976, grants competition has been cancelled.
A number of new programs about to be announced have been shelved for the time being.
Program grants, announced in April 1975, will be initiated in a modest way.
Interim Supply
General research grants have each been reduced by one-third for 1976-77.
A 3 per cent cut will be made in the operating component (exclusive of support provided for approved trainee and professional assistants) of all MRC grants for 1976-77 except term grants in their third year and terminal awards, as well as in the operating components of funds provided to MRC groups, development grants and program grants. A number of terminal awards which would in the past have been of eight months' duration will be reduced to three months.
The number of new scholarships to be offered for 1976-77 will be 15.
The intake to the fellowship program has been reduced from 75 in 1975-76 to 50 in the post-MD, DDS and DVM category and from 55 to 44 in the post Ph.D category-
I understand that the Prime Minister, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the minister responsible for science received close to 500 letters from people in the scientific community. Some scientists were good enough to send copies of letters to members of the opposition. May I quote part of the letter written by Dr. Victor Chernick, professor and head, department of pediatrics, at the children's centre in Winnipeg, and sent to the Prime Minister on March 1, 1976. Dr. Chernick said, in part:
The level of funding for medical research in Canada on a per capita basis is approximately $2 (MRC budget of $50 million) while that in the United States is approximately ten times this rate. Thus, we are in danger of losing our best people, scientists who would compete very favourably in the U.S. funding arena.
May I quote from another letter sent to the Prime Minister on January 29 by Dr. J. C. Haworth, professor of pediatrics, director of clinical investigation and research at the health sciences centre, Winnipeg. He said, in part:
Reduction of our research programs will have the following results ... Since about 70 per cent of our research funding is used to pay salaries, the reduction in the value of research funds will inevitably require the discharge of some technical staff. Quite apart from the personal hardship this will cause, it must be recognized that many of these people are highly trained and skilled in their work and it will take years to train others to the same level of competence when research funds again become more plentiful.
Allow me to quote from another letter which Dr. William A. Bridger, secretary of the Canadian Biochemical Society, sent to the Prime Minister on January 15, 1976. He said, in part:
I wish to express my dismay and frustration, shared by the over 800 members of the Canadian Biochemical Society, which arise from your recently announced freeze upon the budget of the Medical Research Council. The freeze results in a cut of about $7 million from a budget that was already inadequate to the extent that the very survival of a viable medical research establishment in this country was threatened. This cut, together with inflationary pressures upon research budgets which have accumulated over the past few years, can be guaranteed to have profound deleterious effects upon the activities of the Canadian medical research community, with widespread, irreversible ramifications for future medical care that I am sure all thinking Canadians would wish to avoid.
Writing to the Prime Minister of January 26, 1976, D. G. Scraba, associate professor of the department of biochemistry, University of Alberta, said in part:
While I support your government's intention to control its spending, I seriously question its priorities for restraint. Surely the saving of $7 million from the total federal budget cannot justify the harmful immediate and long-term effects upon medical research in this country.
