I raised the very question I am raising at present in the adjournment debate on March 4. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology answered me. I sent a copy of that day's Hansard to Dr. Bridger. Dr. Bridger wrote to the parliamentary secretary. I did not ask him to write; he sent me a copy of his letter. I shall put part of it on record as he, being an expert in the field, can express the concerns of the scientific community more adequately than I can. Dealing with the parliamentary secretary's answer, Dr. Bridger, who was obviously concerned about the effects of the government's freeze on medical research, wrote in part, in his letter dated March 17, 1976, as follows:
You state that "scientific research cannot be an exception" in the effort to reduce inflation. In fact, research councils have been singled out for devastating cuts. While the rest of society is given a ten per cent guideline, the research council budgets for the coming year have been frozen at the fiscal 1975-76 level. Surely you can appreciate that this results directly in a decrease in our research capacity which is precisely equivalent to the rate of inflation, estimated to be nearly 20 per cent in recent surveys of research laboratories. Although excellent cases can be made for expansion of Canada's research effort, we are at the moment falling away behind. And then, you have the audacity to say that-
Dr. Bridger then quoted the words of the parliamentary secretary:
-it certainly does not mean that there will be a dismantling of our research teams.
That is the end of the quotation. The letter goes on to say:
It means exactly that! By 1974 the level of support of research had reached a critically low level; all mediocrity had been weeded out. The present freeze means that about 7 per cent of the research teams in this country, employing over 1,000 highly trained scientists who have survived in the fierce competition until now, will be forced to shut down. Your allegation that the freeze would not have this unavoidable consequence is utterly preposterous.
Allow me to put on record two brief excerpts from the letter sent to the Minister of State for Science and Technology on January 16, 1976, by Keith Yates, professor and chairman, department of chemistry, University of Toronto. He said, in part:
I am writing to you, both as a practising scientist and as chairman of one of the largest university chemistry departments in Canada, to express my grave concern over the steadily deteriorating position of basic science in this country.
He went on to say:
One has only to examine the budgetary treatment of the National Research Council over the past six years to realize that support of basic science in this country has occupied a very low position in terms of federal government priorities. This council, which plays a crucial role for all Canadian university scientists engaged in fundamental research, has received budgetary increases over the period 1970-75 which have fallen far short of increased costs due to inflation. In a period when the Consumer Price Index increased by well over 50 per cent, the NRC budget received cumulative increases totalling only 5.5 per cent. In the

forthcoming budget year (1976-77), when the CPI will probably again increase by more that 10 per cent, the NRC budget will be frozen at the already inadequate 1975-76 level.
The minister suggested that it is not enough to criticize: we ought to show where we can make cuts. Need I remind the minister how much the government spent on Mirabel and of the tens of millions spent on Pickering airport, not needed and not be proceeded with? Each year this government has been in power the Auditor General has listed a tale of horrors. One would hope the government would pay some attention and that some year there would be a lessening of his criticism. After all, it can no longer be said that the Auditor General is a political enemy of the government, that he was appointed by a Conservative government. This government has chosen the Auditor General. He may not be a Liberal, but I am sure they knew when they appointed him that he was not against the Liberals. However, the tale of horror continues about waste, poor management, poor planning and an escalation of senior civil servants, with all that means in the way of salaries, extra secretaries and fancy office space costing hundreds of thousands of dollars which is unused each year because they are not ready for it.
The minister tells us that this is a firm budget and they are determined to hold the line, to show restraint and to make cuts. I hope that from the few remarks I have made it will be obvious to everyone that we in the opposition have every right to say that we are still skeptical about the minister's words.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to take this opportunity of the debate on Bill C-91 to make a few representations to the cabinet and underline once more the needs of the province of Quebec, in particular the region I have the honour to represent. I would like as well to emphasize the fact that in a few areas, the province of Quebec has not reached the level it should have reached in view of the efforts that were made and the propaganda broadcasted on the news both on the CBC network and private stations.
Mr. Chairman, the economic situation of eastern Quebec is such that it requires immediate action from the central government. I am really staggered when I hear entirely contradictory news, as I did yesterday on the CBC. The Quebec Minister of Industry and Commerce, on one hand, was asserting that the province of Quebec is experiencing a real growth and that the economy of the province has never been so flourishing. A moment later, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) whom I respect for his frankness, after looking at his department's report, deplored the fact that the province of Quebec is lagging behind other provinces, that its per capita income is lower and that industrial development is slower than in the other provinces.
I will take this opportunity to make a comment that I wish to be as kind as possible. I heard in the House from some of my colleagues comments to the effect that the federal government is in the hands of the French power. The French power would mean that the federal cabinet is governing first and above all according to the interests of
March 25, 1976

the province of Quebec, the only French-speaking province in this country. And yet, if one looks at statistics, one sees that this French power is not acting only in the interests of the province of Quebec since the latter is lagging behind other provinces.
At any rate, Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to raise a debate which might jeopardize or eliminate the unity that must exist in our country. We are first of all Canadians. We also have different cultures. We have two official languages: English and French. Both have the same rights in this country and in this Parliament, and I think we would be wasting very precious time if we were to discuss those questions which were settled many years ago and to which we should not come back. But still there are economic problems, and the interests of the French-speaking or English-speaking people are absolutely the same in this country. I have never seen a $20 bill speaking either English or French; the $20 bill speaks both languages.
We also need an income, both in the east and in the west, to enable each Canadian to meet his obligations, to buy the things necessary to satisfy his personal needs at the individual, family and community level.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I find inacceptable these glaring contradictions between the statements of a French-speaking minister of the Parliament of Canada and those of a minister of the National Assembly of Quebec on the same subject, who analyzed the situation and came to completely opposite conclusions. And if I consider the budget of the Canadian government, the budget allocated to each province of our country, I find it equitably distributed, but still it remains the duty of the Canadian government, of the Canadian Parliament, to see if there is an equitable distribution among the regions of Canada, whatever the province in which they are.
The Gaspe peninsula, the south shore of the St. Lawrence, the Quebec City area, and the province of Quebec within Canada, deserve as much attention from the Canadian government as the Vancouver or Victoria areas, or the Maritime provinces. To my mind, our role consists in administering funds without consideration of race or religion. We must see to it that the budget of the Canadian government is shared equitably, taking into consideration the needs of each area, whether it is inhabited by Francophones or Anglophones. That is how I see things, Mr. Chairman.
Now, this is what happens: the province of Quebec has transportation problems that may not exist elsewhere. That is what brings me to speak of the wharves located along the St. Lawrence river which help communications between those who live out on the islands and those who live on the mainland. At the present time, Mr. Chairman, there is a quarrel going on between the federal and Quebec provincial governments, about whether the wharves located in the province of Quebec, along the St. Lawrence, should be considered part of the highway network of the province. If so, responsibility for their maintenance should fall to the province. The federal and provincial governments have set a body to look into the matter and share responsibilities; according to my information, the Quebec government is quite willing to accept the responsibility for the maintenance of those wharves as part of its highway network conditional upon the central government's first
Interim Supply
repairing them before handing them over to the province for future maintenance. That is the bone of contention, Mr. Chairman.
This afternoon I communicated with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) and I asked him some clarification about the items contained in Bill C-91 which request a borrowing power of $6 billion. That is quite a lot of money, Mr. Chairman. Can we hope that with these $6 billion, the central government, through the Department of Public Works, will make improvements to the wharves along the St. Lawrence and on the islands of the St. Lawrence which need maintenance work to remain operative? I am not talking about wharves which should be maintained because of their history, for instance, but about those that have to be used regularly to maintain constant communications between the islands and the mainland.
The minister, who is an intelligent and an honest man, did not want to give me any definite answer. He simply gave me a note saying that he would review the program and that if the wharves in Bellechasse-and Bellechasse is part of Canada as far as I know-are included in the estimates, part of the budgetary items will be used to upgrade the wharves which need it, and this would come under this borrowing power of $6 billion.
Mr. Chairman, if this is the case, I shall be glad to support this bill. This money is needed to effect these improvements, to upgrade the wharves. There should be an agreement with the Quebec government for these wharves to be properly maintained, and come in the future under the jurisdiction of the Quebec government as part of the Quebec network. I am in complete agreement on this point. However, it matters little where these billions of dollars come from; this is something that must be discussed. I hope that this year, when Parliament studies the legislation giving chartered banks the power to create credit and to loan money to the population, we shall discuss this issue. However, for the time being, Mr. Chairman, it is my duty to support this budget item if they agree to use that money to solve a problem which has been swept under the carpet for too long. I very much hope that the Minister of Public Works will take into account the representations I am making now so that this matter can be solved once and for all.
A second point I would like to make in this debate is the federal-provincial agreements on the economic development of our country. There is an absolute necessity for the central government to sign agreements with the governments of all provinces, because the provinces are regional administrations closer to the people and they are in a better position to determine the real priorities for Canadians.
I wish that the central government could speed up all forms of negotiations. Not that the central government should impose its views on provincial governments but negotiations should be conducted on a meaningful basis. People appointed by the government or by ministers of various departments-civil servants, the senior civil servants of our administration-should understand once for all how urgent it is for Canada's unity to expedite those negotiations as people become impatient. The public at

Interim Supply
large cannot understand in every detail the various forms of negotiations and it gets impatient.
Sometimes, Mr. Chairman, some elements of our population take advantage of the slowness of negotiation to raise linguistic, racial and regional issues likely to divide Canadians further instead of uniting them so that all together we could work seriously and efficiently toward the development and prosperity of our country.
Mr. Chairman, within our parliamentary duties we sometimes have the unique opportunity to visit other countries as delegates. Mr. Chairman, in countries we only know by name and whose customs are unknown to us, we can see that people of all races are living there, black, white, orientals, Indians, people who speak several languages and who succeed in living and working together.
I wish to mention Mauritius that I visited last fall. Those people succeed in working together for the prosperity of their country.
Mr. Chairman, I would be very glad if we could do the same in this country. Whether we eat in French, in English, in German or in Italian, whatever the language we use, we must always keep in mind that we are first and above all Canadians.
Mr. Chairman, in my opinion, Canada is the most beautiful country in the world. In spite of our hard winters, of our snow, we still have four seasons we should be proud of. If Canada is to continue its development and growth for the profit of all the people who live in it, we must of necessity cooperate. We must work together and, as Canadian parliamentarians, we must always keep in mind that we must administer the revenue of our country by distributing it equitably.
Mr. Chairman, I make these remarks so that we can have a fair distribution in Quebec.
It does not matter whether we are Liberals, Conservatives, members of the Social Credit Party or members of the New Democratic Party. What matters is that we can say to the Canadian people that we made what we could to have a fair distribution of incomes between Canadians so that each area of the country has its shares and that we can say proudly: Canada is developing all its areas, regardless of our language.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure those members who know me in the House will recognize that I will not be partisan during this debate. I do want to indicate my very grave concern about this science policy for Canada, and particularly that component that deals with medical research.
The minister in his comments which, if I may say so, were of a highly political form, has indicated a program of restraint. I have no difficulty in identifying with that. I think he should also note the importance of research and development in terms of the productivity about which he talked. Of course, whether it be in economic terms or in human terms, research and development in my opinion, and I think in the opinion of many, are an investment in the future.

If one wanted to dramatize the importance of medical research I think all he would have to do is point to the questions which were raised in the House today, and I am referring specifically to the problem of swine influenza and the recent announcement of the President of the United States, who indicated his administration will be introducing a comprehensive program to prevent the outbreak of this particular disease. I only need to refer to the great epidemic of 1916-18 in which 15 million to 18 million lives were lost. May I simply say that without medical research and without the bio-medical community, that type of commodity and that type of progress would not be with us today.
At the outset I want to quote, if I may, from an article which states:
It is difficult to realize at such short range just how important an influence the work of Dr. Banting and Mr. Best has been in stimulating medical research in Canada, and indeed throughout the civilized world; but it seems likely that history will view the discovery of insulin, not only as a valuable contribution to the science of medicine but of peculiar significance in as much as the efforts of several ancillary sciences were focused upon its discovery. In a peculiar way, therefore, the work of Banting and Best represents medical research at its highest. So far as Canada is concerned we may be forgiven our special pride, in that our owns sons, in our own country, have produced something so worthy of the noblest traditions of our calling, and that their discovery was given freely to the whole world. We are well aware that Canada has produced many exceptional men of science, but only too many whose contributions have brought renown alone to the countries of their adoption, rather than to the land of their education and birth.
That editorial appeared in the CMA Journal in 1923, and it depicted the spirit of our pioneers in the bio-medical research community. It also, of course, outlined the successes of that particular day. We have seen that spirit throughout the 1960's, but I want to say with all sincerity that in recent years we have seen the strangulation of that pioneering spirit, with a very demoralizing effect on the medical research community in Canada.
I have followed with great interest and concern the Ministry of Science and Technology, and in particular the Medical Research Council. I have done this, as I indicated, with great concern since my arrival in Ottawa as a member of parliament in 1972. I think one can best describe the system, in my experience, as one of action, reaction, confrontation, and innumerable committee reports; in fact, a constant upheaval regarding the funding of research and, in particular, medical research in Canada, something that is most undesirable where stability is required.
I was prepared at the outset today to argue that the Medical Research Council requires an additional 15 per cent to 20 per cent in funding for the coming fiscal year, and I believe I would have no difficulty in presenting that argument. However, after hearing the President of the Treasury Board speak I have no intention of entering into the numbers game at this particular time, which in my view would be counterproductive when the government is employing political tactics to give the impression that it is actually introducing measures of economic restraint but without any consideration of priorities.
Let me make it very clear, and I want to make this very clear so there is no misunderstanding among hon. members in this Chamber, that if in fact the federal government had a national policy for science, and if in fact the federal government had a national policy in respect of health
March 25, 1976

research, and medical research in particular, then I would suggest to you in all sincerity that this debate would not have been necessary today. It would have been redundant and, indeed, the scientific community would have had adequate funds to carry out its particular disciplines.
As the scenario of government inaction in developing policy and the demoralizing confrontation with the scientific community have unfolded, one fact has become perfectly clear. The scientists for their part have a good deal to learn about policy and the political process; and the government and, I say in all sincerity, the bureaucracy of mandarins associated with it, have a great deal to learn about science. I have no doubt that if dialogue between the two parties I have mentioned had been better, and if the government has seen fit to establish a mechanism for an ongoing exchange of views, a realistic and effective science policy would have been established. As I indicated previously, this debate would have been redundant and unnecessary.
I indicated that scientists have a good deal to learn about policy and the political process. Frankly I have some degree of sympathy with that section of the scientific community which believes they must devote their efforts to their primary work rather than being involved in the political arena. However, the recent experience of representatives of the Canadian Society of Clinical Investigations at their meeting in Quebec, and their dealings with the press, are an example of an unfortunate communications gap that can occur and be very detrimental to their cause. Without attempting to defend their action I believe that many scientists are afraid of the media and have found the political process to be frustrating, time-consuming, and non-productive.
On a more positive note I wish to emphasize the importance of good communications and to state that this was demonstrated very ably by a Dr. John Bienenstock of McMaster, and Dr. Charles Schriber of Montreal, when they appeared as witnesses before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, and articulated in a positive manner the concerns of the research community.
I submit to the government, Mr. Speaker, that this is the type of dialogue that is extremely important. I indicated that the government and the mandarins associated with the government have a great deal to learn about science. I wish to take a moment or two to mention briefly a few principles I feel are important, principles which I believe the government has not grasped and does not understand in the whole field of scientific endeavour.
In the area of health I do not think anyone would argue that the ultimate goal of all health research is to improve the health of each Canadian. Society expects, and we have the responsibility to assure high standards of medical education, health services, and health care. Research is linked to the training of professional manpower, to learning, and to a high quality health care system, and is therefore dependent on a viable research base. I find it inconceivable that the government cannot understand this very simple fundamental principle that medical research is interrelated with medical education, which in turn is related to the quality of medical care that is given Canadians.
Interim Supply
If I may, Mr. Chairman, in relation to this particular aspect I should like to quote from an article by Dr. J. B. Armstrong entitled "Quality Teaching, Care Depends on Research". I should point out that Dr. Armstrong is Chief Medical Adviser to the Canadian Heart Foundation. The article states:
Scientific research is a part of the culture and has a role not unlike creative activity in the arts. But it has an additional function, a dividend if you will, in the expansion of knowledge as well as experience. Scientific research is thus a learning experience, of asking questions and seeking answers. Research in the humanities tends to rely on interpretation of the work of others, that is, library research as distinct from the bench research of the natural sciences. My point is that scholarly research is a creative learning experience for the worker and at the same time adds to the general fund of knowledge.
The learning aspect of research is a most important component of university activity, where most of the organized higher learning now takes place. Medical knowledge is no exception. It is growing very rapidly, almost certainly doubling in less than every five years. To keep abreast of this rapid expansion, the learning process in Canadian health centres requires that our imaginative teachers be learners also, at the threshold of their particular fields of endeavour. This form of learning in our medical schools is medical research. The recognition of this learning component by MRC and other health agencies has meant that the distribution of grants and awards has offset, to a degree, regional disparities. It is essential to the continued development of health care in Canada.
Again I must re-emphasize the very fundamental principle, which has not grasped by the government or by the ministers on the opposite side, that medical research and medical education are involved with the delivery of quality health care. I have no intention of developing the arguments in respect of basic or pure research versus applied research or mission oriented research since I believe there is an important role for each of these areas. I think it is clear that we must establish some priorities which require urgent attention, and therefore there must be appropriate research programs for this. However, I must also point out that in my opinion we must ensure an adequate freedom for the researchers in our community.
In this regard I was particularly disturbed by a recent article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of Thursday, March 18, 1976. It is entitled "Scientists Come Out Fighting as Research Money Frozen". I wish to quote the article as follows:
Science Minister C. M. Drury recently told the Senate science policy committee that science and technology should be supported 'to the extent that it can serve to resolve the problems we face, social or national problems. The extent to which it would exist for and in itself is, in my mind, a great deal more doubtful.' Mr. Drury argued against a 'blind faith' in science as 'a good thing'. If science and technology can be helpful 'it should be supported,' he said, 'and if it can't it shouldn't.'
I realize that newspapers at times have been known to misquote, but I want to remind hon. members that in the throne speech of 1973, at which time the science policy was espoused, on that day there was no doubt in my mind, or in the minds of these who followed it closely, that the decision of the government was in fact to make certain that the various research councils and the various granting bodies should more directly serve its own policy objectives.
I know there are many individuals in all parts of this House who believe there is no room for basic research or for curiosity research. However, I want to suggest this is a very dangerous assumption. I would simply refer to the present classification that is used in terms of grants. As I understand it there are three classifications. There is type

March 25, 1976
Interim Supply
I,	referred to as curiosity-oriented research. There is a type
II,	which is real research for support of departmental goals. Finally, there is research for the support of national objectives. If one looks at this very carefully one will see there are certain dangers.
I want to emphasize that I believe in theory there is some merit to this type of approach. For example, I know that curiosity-oriented research or so-called pure research can be and is evaluated by the peer review mechanism guaranteeing scientific excellence. The danger, of course, is when the politician or bureaucrat, or some other individual raises the priority rating of a scientifically inadequate type of program and is prepared to make it fundable under a type II program. Of course we have the situation where the pure science will be pursued for political reasons, and of course in such an instance, in my opinion, everyone will lose.
Before closing I should like to quote what I think is a very worthwhile comment by Albert Szent-Gyorgyi in an article on research grants which appeared in "Perspectives in Biology and Medicine-Autumn 1974". I should point out that Albert Szent-Gyorgyi was the Nobel Laureate for the discovery of Vitamin C. It states:
Scientific research is, in many ways, related to art. If one wants good music to be produced, one looks for a good musician and not for a project. Projects have no meaning and value anyway, because there are only two kinds of science: good and bad. Good science is made by good scientists, poor science by poor scientists, and the most brillant project is worthless in the hands of a poor scientist, while, conversely, a good scientist has a good chance to come up with something valuable whatever he touches, because "die Welt rundet sich im Tautrophen" (Goethe) which could be translated by saying that all the great laws of nature are represented in a drop of dew. Pasteur went to Germany to study brewing beer and came home with the discovery of optical isomerism.
It is easy to find good scientists, because the good scientists are mostly those who have produced good science. Find them and support them, enable them to work. That's all there is to it. Don't torture them with senseless projects.
Let me simply say in conclusion that the entire problem related to medical research, to the science policy in Canada, is, in my opinion, more than the need for a temporary transfusion of funds. I believe it requires an understanding, a grasp of the problems of science and its importance in our community, and a recognition on the part of the government of the importance of science in our community and to Canadian citizens. Finally, it requires a commitment to develop that type of science policy.

I wish to express my thanks to the hon. member for Scarborough East for yielding the floor, and also to the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton for his courtesy with regard to the arrangements which were made.
My statement is with respect to clause 5 of the interim supply bill which, as hon. members know, seeks new statutory borrowing authority of $6 billion and would serve the purpose of cancelling all outstanding and unused borrowing authority.
As hon. members are aware, the Financial Administration Act, section 36, requires that no money shall be borrowed or security issued by or on behalf of Her Majesty without the authority of parliament. This refers to new money only, because there is a continuing authority in the act for the government to borrow funds to repay maturing debt. Authority to borrow sufficient new money to cover estimated financial requirements, together with a margin for contingencies, is normally sought and granted in one of the first appropriation acts of any fiscal year.
Hon. members might find it helpful if I begin by reviewing the situation in fiscal 1975-76, which will come to an end in a few days time. It will be recalled that a borrowing authority of $4 billion is provided in Appropriation Act No. 2 for 1975, and a further $2 billion in the Supplementary Borrowing Authority Act 1975. Under this total authority of $6 billion we have obtained net new money of $4.6 billion this fiscal year, and a further $214 million will be obtained from the April 1 bond issue. Thus the unused authority which will be cancelled by the passage of the bill will amount to about $1.2 billion.
In sum, by March 31, 1976, the increases in debt issues will be as follows: treasury bills, $865 million; Canada savings bonds, $2,600 million; marketable bonds, $1,175 million, making a total of $4,640 million. The amounts offered at the 90 day and 180 day treasury bill auctions
Interim Supply
were increased, starting a year ago, at the rate of $10 million per week, and this subsequently increased in July to $15 million, and in October to $20 million.
After a pause during the Canada Savings Bond campaign the program was reinstituted with a weekly offer of $20 million, and this figure is now $25 million. The one year bills were auctioned four times during the year, with increments totalling $150 million over the period.
In fiscal 1975-76, $1,774 million in marketable bonds matured, and in exchange $2,550 million worth of bonds were sold. In August a gap in the maturity schedule was used to raise a further $400 million of new money. Emphasis was placed during the year on raising money on the long term bond market, and it proved possible to build up a $600 million single issue maturing October 1, 1995.
The 1975-76 Canada Savings Bond program was most successful with gross sales of about $3,700 million, while redemptions over the fiscal year totalled about $1,100 million. It will be noted that the Canada Saving Bonds total has been maintained at approximately 39 per cent of the total government debt.
The ownership of the debt has changed slightly over the year. The chartered banks own about $100 million more, while the Bank of Canada has increased its holdings by $800 million. The public has purchased about $1 billion of marketable securities and treasury bills as well as $2.5 billion of Canada Savings Bonds.
The $4.6 billion we borrowed has been more than sufficient to meet our requirements. Our cash balances amounted to $3.2 billion at the beginning of the year and stood at $3.7 billion as of yesterday, an increase of $500 million. Thus our total financial requirements have amounted to $4 billion. Excluding foreign exchange transactions which have, on balance, been a source of funds, our financial requirements have been $4.3 billion.
We expect a substantial rundown in cash balances in the remaining few days of the fiscal year. A number of large payments will be made, and the volume of tax refunds is building. I cannot be precise about the final figure for the fiscal year but it seems likely that the total financial requirements will be at the lower end of the range of $5 billion to $6 billion.
I would remind hon. members that the books remain open for a period of time after the end of the fiscal year and thus some months will elapse before the detailed accounts showing the breakdown between budgetary and non-budgetary transactions will be prepared. I will provide the House with preliminary estimates in my budget in May.
Turning to the fiscal year 1976-77, my colleague, the President of the Treasury Board, has indicated that total outlays for the fiscal year will be $42,150 million, an increase of a little less than 16 per cent. The main estimates have of course been tabled in the House and are being examined in detail by the standing committees. It seems likely that our revenues will grow by broadly similar amounts as our outlays, on the basis of the existing tax structure and the widespread expectation that real growth

March 25, 1976
Interim Supply
in the economy will amount to about 5 per cent and the rate of inflation will decline.
On this basis, the total financial requirements will be of the same order of magnitude next year as in 1975-76. I will of course be providing more precise and detailed forecasts in my budget, taking into account the latest information available on the economy and any policy tax changes to be announced at that time.
As in 1975-76, we may be able to meet some of our requirements by running down cash balances, since they are likely to be at a comfortable level, even after the drain of the next few days. I can thus visualize a public debt program for 1976-77 of broadly similar magnitude and composition as in 1975-76.
The borrowing authority of $6 billion being sought by the government under this bill is the same as that obtained in 1975-76, and provides the necessary margin for contingencies. The financial requirements excluding foreign exchange transactions may be larger than can now be foreseen. Foreign exchange transactions are impossible to predict. If the Canadian dollar is strong in the exchange markets, our ongoing policy of intervention in order to maintain orderly market conditions can add significantly to our cash requirements as they have done recently. It is of course also the case that the sale of foreign exchange can provide a source of money for us when the value of the Canadian dollar is declining.
Finally, I would note that we cannot control with great precision the amounts of Canada Savings Bonds which the public will buy each year. Successful campaigns as in the past two years can exhaust the borrowing authority if no margin is provided.
That is a review of the use of the borrowing authority in the fiscal year just closing and some perspective on the borrowing authority now being sought on an interim basis in this bill.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister could tell the House what the cumulative borrowing authority to the government is at the present time, bearing in mind the two appropriation bills he referred to which were both passed in 1975?

Mr. Chairman, in my remarks I just indicated that it came to an aggregate of $6 billion-$4 billion provided in Appropriation Act No. 2 of 1975, and a further $2 billion in the Supplementary Borrowing Authority Act of 1975.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister misunderstood my question. The wording of the two appropriation acts that I referred to is that the government has the authority to negotiate loans, etc. to the extent of the $6 billion that he refers to, but in addition they can also carry all the debt that is on the books. What I want is a figure of the total debt, plus the additional authority made available to the government.

Mr. Chairman, the figure of the total outstanding debt was given in the standing committee. I do not have it with me this evening. Both the government's funded debt and other liabilities-as up to date figures as were then available-were given to the hon.

member in the standing committee. I would have to check the debt review to give that exact figure. To repeat my answer, however, the authorization for 1975-76 was $6 billion.
I take it the figure that the minister is referring to is the one given at the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs on March 18.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. The last time the hon. member and I addressed this issue, and I am not sure of the exact date, my officials were there and made the calculation as near as one can do at the moment, on the outstanding debt. My recollection is it was as of March 31, 1975, and the more up to date figure of March 31, 1976 which was necessarily an estimate, and the estimated average between the two figures.

Further on a point of clarification, Mr. Chairman, the debt figures given by the minister at that committee meeting are the debt figures in relation to interest bearing debt. Do I take it that clause 5 gives authorization only in reference to interest bearing debt and does not include the total gross debt of the country which at March 31, 1975, for example, was $62.6 billion?

Clause 5 provides authority to borrow on such terms either by interest or discount as may be arranged in the market by the Bank of Canada as agent for the Government of Canada. Other debts that the government may have under the Canada Pension Plan, armed forces superannuation and other plans are not included in this authority to borrow. This is authority to borrow for the purpose of government expenditures.

May I take it from the minister's remarks that liabilities that are reflected on Canada's balance sheet in a liability and assets sense, liabilities that are not interest bearing, are not included in the gross debt figures that are contemplated in clause 5?

There are liabilities of various kinds in regard to various departments. What we have been talking about are the liabilities for which I am responsible as Minister of Finance under the Department of Finance. Other outstanding liabilities, either on current terms or otherwise, would have to be found from the various departments themselves.
For example, if the hon. member is referring to unliquidated claims that might be recovered against the Government of Canada under the Crown Liability Act in the Federal Court of Canada, of course one cannot make any estimate in advance of what damages the courts may award against the government for motor vehicle negligence or other liabilities. We are talking exclusively of authority to borrow funds for the purpose of the Crown meeting the expenditures of the Government of Canada in 1976-77.

If I may refer again to the meeting of the standing committee to which the minister has referred and the figures given by the minister that day, as of March 31, 1976, the interest bearing debt of the nation was $53,667 million. Mr. Chairman, I realize time is running out so I shall be brief. During this discussion of the estimates of the President of the Treasury Board I wish to call attention to a pay practice which I consider to be unfair to those employees of the government known as casuals. I am addressing this point to the minister in his capacity as representing the government as employer. It is somewhat in the nature of a grievance felt by many people in my constituency, and undoubtedly by constituents of other members. The grievance arise from the regulations administered by Treasury Board relating to the retroactive pay of casuals. The problem can be simply stated.
First, as members well know, casuals are not included in the collective bargaining process nor do they enjoy certain other benefits available to permanent employees of the government. The question I want to raise for hon. members is this: should these differences in the status of casuals and other employees justify the present rule that casuals do not qualify for retroactive pay when, for example, they have worked during a period after a collective agreement has expired and before a new one is negotiated? I do not think they should be excluded from retroactive pay because of their different status.

For example, let us assume that an agreement expired last November and that the new agreement was ratified in February, with a three-month period following termination of the agreement. Those who are classified as permanent employees, or even as term casuals, will receive retroactive pay for the three months' period after the agreement terminated. This is not the case with casuals unless a casual had worked in an uninterrupted fashion for the preceding six months.
It is this six-month formula or rule that I wish to raise as a grievance before we pass the estimates. I believe this produces an injustice, and what I am doing is making a representation to the President of the Treasury Board, asking him to consider changing the formula. Let us consider perhaps a typical case, and then I should like to suggest to the minister an amended formula.
Consider a casual during any given year who works for perhaps three weeks and is then laid off, comes back on the payroll for two months and is then laid off, comes back on the payroll for a few weeks and is laid off, and comes back on the payroll for six months and is laid off. That is a typical pattern under which casuals operate now.
These are valuable employees if only in that they give flexibility to the employment needs of the government. They assist the government in its work during peak periods and they are not employed at other periods but in effect are on standby. This is of benefit to the employees who wish to be in the casual category, and is of benefit to the government, particularly to certain departments which have seasonal loads, for example National Health and Welfare, the Post Office, the Unemployment Insurance Commission undoubtedly, as well as other departments where there is an unsteady rhythm of employment needs.
The pay for these casuals is in fact related to that of a permanent employee in a similar category. Let us say it is to the second level or the minimum level of a clerk, grade 1, 2 or 3, whatever the cross-reference is. When the pay of one of these permanent employees is raised and there is a retroactive feature, that permanent employee receives retroactive pay, but the casual employee who is linked in a pay fashion to that level does not receive the retroactive pay for the same period. This is a grievance. This is unfair, in my view. It is unjust, and it is more keenly felt during a period of inflation.
My suggestion to the minister would be that the six-month rule be changed. There may be various formulas for the change, but the one I should like to suggest for his consideration is that a casual employee be entitled to retroactivity if the casual employee has worked for a six-month period, whether or not interrupted, in the 12 months preceding the termination of the agreement.
That would be a definite improvement because it would mean that the casual could accumulate six months over the year preceding termination. The employee might accumulate three months, then break off, then three weeks, and so on. There may be other formulas but this is the principle I am seeking, that these people be entitled to retroactivity on a less restrictive and more just formula than the one now existing.

My prime interest, aside from deflating some of this inflationary talk or deflationary talk, is to concern myself with some of the defects in the planning over the last umpteen years by the government in the matter of air-sea rescue on the west coast.
Last year ten fishermen were lost during the herringfishing season off the west coast. There were 14 vessels lost and six more seriously damaged. That was in March, 1975. With some prompting the Department of Transport set up an inquiry in mid-April. By July, after further prompting, a report was finally tabled in this House. It was a good report. It contained some excellent recommendations. Some were for immediate application, certainly before the next herring fishing season which began earlier this month.
Were these recommendations ever implemented before the fishing fleet set out to sea earlier this month, because four more lives already have been lost this season on the herring fishing grounds? Two of these lives were lost on Monday night this week. Against this background the following facts have a great relevance.
There are three service helicopters for air-sea rescue on the west coast, in addition to the one single coast guard helicopter. Of the three service helicopters, as of this morning only one was serviceable. In other words, two helicopters are in service at this moment to be available on call for the fishing fleet at sea composed of hundreds of small vessels spread up and down the coast.
What is more, the helicopter situation is not better this year than it was last year. This brings up the subject of today's debate-the lack of foresight by the government which places us in this perilous position of having too little in the way of air-sea rescue capability on the west coast. I am inclined to think the situation is not much better on the east coast, but we will hear about that shortly.
There is another element in this situation which deserves some comment. The three service helicopters, the three normally available at Comox, are by priority assigned to land search or to sea search for an aircraft downed at sea. They are not necessarily available for air-sea rescue for fishermen in distress. This means that on the west coast only one helicopter with hoist capacity is available, when serviceable, for the saving of life at sea in the Pacific in respect of the fishing fleet.
I should like to revert for a moment to the Fishing Boat Casualty Report which I mentioned earlier. In that report dated March, 1975, but not released to parliament until well on into July, and only then because of continual prodding by me, the officers of the Department of Transport inquiring into last year's accidents made a number of far-reaching recommendations. These recommendations related to training for skippers and mates, the publication of a fishermen's safety pamphlet for seamen generally, as well as weather forecasting, stability and load restrictions and arrangements.
I have had occasion to review these recommendations during the past few days because of the accidents that took place. I wonder how many of these recommendations were ever implemented. I found them all to be excellent and

practical recommendations, but were they implemented? That is what I want to know. If they were not implemented, what was the reason. We lost 14 men and ten vessels last year, and four more men early this year, partly I suspect because these recommendations were not implemented.
Early in January the fishermen made representations to B.C. members of parliament about the forthcoming fishing season. I have a copy of those representations as conveyed to the Minister of Transport by my colleague, the hon. member for Victoria. Some of the recommendations made by the fishermen are identical to those made by the committee of enquiry. These include stability testing, loading arrangements and so on. Aside from this there was a call for improved air-sea rescue facilities for the fishing area. Was any heed paid to this call for help? How much heed was paid to the recommendations that were presented to the minister in January?
The first of the fishing boat disasters this year occurred off Cape Beale, the southern lip of Barclay Sound. Who came to the rescue? The United States Coast Guard. I believe one of their helicopters-and this I find distressing-crashed into the sea in its attempt to rescue some of our Canadian fishermen. We are fortunate in having neighbours of that kind. Two fishermen and the helicopter crew were saved as a result of the activities of a lifeboat crew which put out to sea. Most of the helicopter itself was eventually salvaged, but one seaman was lost and more would have been lost had it not been for the U.S. coastguard. Is there any better way of pointing out the deficiencies of the Canadian coastguard and the Canadian air-sea rescue facilities on the west coast?
I have said it before and I say it again now, hopefully for the last time, that we do not have an effective air-sea rescue on our coast. What is at issue here is a combination of the improper assignment of priorities in budgeting over the last eight or ten years, lack of foresight, and a confusion in the co-ordination of command. If these shortcomings had not been allowed to occur four, five or six years ago, we would not be in the position we are in today, that is, of asking the government to re-examine its priorities so that everything necessary is done to protect the lives of our fishermen.
Strengthening the air-sea rescue capability will cost a lot of money, but lives are at stake. Implementation of the recommendations of the Department of Transport will cost less money, but lives are still at stake, and the recommendations deserve to be implemented. This failure of the government to assign priorities properly adds to the growing fund of lack of confidence which marks the history of the government. Unfortunately this lack of confidence also reflects on parliament and on its members.
The government's credibility is in question, not only as a result of its failure to take the necessary steps in time vis-a-vis air-sea rescue. It has also been considerably shaken, I suggest, as a result of the failure of normal ethical standards of conduct to exercise their expected effect on all members of the cabinet, leading to the commission of what has come to be called impropriety. The experiment in * which we are engaged today as a means of re-examining the estimates is long overdue. It is not absolutely clear whether it will be effective, but something effective has to be worked out to restore the credibility of parliament and of governments in general.
Last evening, for example, as we were asked to approve supplementary estimates we found it absolutely impossible to amend in any way the sums proposed by the government. There was one sum in particular which did not need to be there at all, yet we could not remove it. We were told that we should have had it removed in committee and brought forward to the House as an amendment when reporting the estimates to the House. That had been tried, Mr. Chairman. An opposition motion was put in the committee aimed at dropping that particular sum from the estimates. It was a sum which a senior public servant said he would not need, a matter of some $186,000 to be dropped. What happened? The government members voted to a man to oppose that deletion. As a majority their will prevailed, and as a result we passed in the supplementaries last night a sum of $186,000 which will not be needed.
It was maintained at the time that the unused funds would be returned in the normal course of events to the consolidated revenue fund. This is not necessarily so because in another committee, one on which I sat, some $858,000 of funds voted by this parliament to cover capital costs were admitted to have been diverted to the payment of services. When we questioned this improper procedure we were told that permission to cover this diversion was actually being asked at that moment. But if you examined those supplementaries, those funds had already been spent. So we cannot be absolutely certain that the $186,000 which was overestimated would be returned to the consolidated revenue fund automatically. This is one of the reasons why we are having this particular experiment in procedure tonight.
We want to devise methods of improving control by parliament over expenditures by government of whatever kind. What we want to know is where the government places its priorities in relation to expenditures of public funds, and in particular in the case of which I spoke, in relation to the safety of life at sea. There has been no evidence over the past three or four years, even after the tragedies of last year, that priorities in this area have been adjusted to meet altering demands.
In the matter of co-ordination of effort to bring together the activities of all the departments concerned, such as the Department of Transport, the Department of the Environment, the Department of Fisheries, the Solicitor General's Department, the RCMP, the Department of National Defence, and even Customs, little has been done to meet these crying needs. I am disturbed that the government is so bankrupt in the matter of governing that it will permit this parliament and the whole democratic process to become so eroded that we will have to start again at the beginning to restore parliament and all its institutions to the respect and honour which an effective performance alone can produce.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to terminate my comments which I started a little earlier. I yielded my place to allow the discussion to continue on clause 5. I was discussing the terms of reference given some two years to the committee which appear in the report of the Auditor General on financial management and control practices within the government. I should like to read these terms of reference into the record because of their new application to the estimates process which we are now going through.
The committee was asked to examine:
(a)	Statutes and Treasury Board regulations, policies, directives and guidelines relevant to financial management and control, and the extent of compliance therewith in departments and agencies;
(b)	Financial systems and procedures in departments and agencies including budgetary controls, accounting for revenues, expenditures, assets, liabilities, commitments, and financial reporting systems;
(c)	Integration of the departmental and agency accounting processes and systems with the central systems;
(d)	Extent to which the financial systems and procedures are monitored and audited by internal or operational audit groups;
(e)	Type, accuracy, timeliness, purpose and use of financial information and reports currently prepared;
(f)	Extent of decentralization following on the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Government Organization and its impact on over-all financial control, and
(g)	Duties, responsibilities and functions of financial and accounting managers and staff with special reference to the system of financial and accounting control and the relationships of their function with central financial and accounting agencies.
I think it is important also that these terms of reference, as I mentioned earlier, were very encompassing and provided the largest investigation into financial management and control within government organization that has taken place since the Glassco Commission was appointed some 15 years ago.
In the time available to me tonight I should like to cover one or two of the major recommendations from that study, and I emphasize again that the study is only half completed. I will be brief because I know others want to participate in this debate. To the present time the study has only dealt with individual government departments. The next part of the study will deal with Crown corporations and their many agencies operated under the government.
One of the key recommendations from this study is that no longer is it recommended that three departments continue to hold the joint responsibility for the financing, management, and control of accounting procedures and procedures relating to preparation of estimates in the government. Indeed up until now it has been the practice that this responsibility has been shared by the Department of Supply and Services, the Treasury Board, and the Department of Finance.
In large industry-and government is a large organization-it is accepted that there must be centralization of

financial control at some point. This particular study in its report recommends that this responsibility pass entirely to the Treasury Board. In future-and this is the recommendation which the President of the Treasury Board has unequivocally indicated will certainly be accepted by the government-there will be one department in government, the Treasury Board, which will assume this central responsibility for financial management and control.
I think it is important also to note that there has been a recommendation by this committee that there be more consideration in the formation of estimates, starting at the top and working down. This is not intended to take away the incentive of the people working out in the field and at the lower levels of government to come up with the kinds of programs which they think it would be proper and desirable to implement. What it does say, however, is that at some point there is to be a cap put on. In other words, that cap will be put on at the top, and individual ideas being worked upon from the bottom up will have to be sifted at some point so that indeed they can fit into the over-all total which can be ascribed to that particular department. I think this is important because there has been a tendency in the past, in the massive growth of government bureaucracy we have seen, for programs to come up from the bottom, and it has been difficult to ascertain just what cap has been applied. This is an important recommendation.
Another important recommendation on which there may still be some difference in interpretation is the matter of the appointment of a chief financial officer with the government. I believe it is the idea of the study group that a person should be designated chief financial officer at some point, just as we find is done in large corporate undertakings. Regardless of the total number of people who have financial control, somewhere in a corporate entity there is one chief financial officer who ultimately must answer to the brass, as it were, for what is happening in terms of the financial operation of that undertaking.
I believe that at the moment the Treasury Board is of the opinion that the Treasury Board as a collective unit is the chief financial officer, and I think this is something which needs to be explored still further.
Of the three studies I mentioned earlier I think this study is being put before the Public Accounts Committee and is the most important in terms of over-all purview of government financial operations in years to come. It will take many years to implement in its entirety, and the understanding of those of us in the Public Accounts Committee at the present time is that there are only two recommendations with which the Treasury Board tends to disagree. There are perhaps seven or eight recommendations with which the Treasury Board agrees, and a number over which there is substantial agreement.
For the purposes of the record, the recommendations in the study are contained in chapter 10 of the report of the Auditor General for the year ended March 31, 1975. This particular chapter is so significant that I believe for the first time in recent years the Auditor General found it necessary to bring out a supplement of some 300 pages to back up strictly that one chapter of his report for the year ended March 31, 1975. There are many other recommendations I should have liked to talk about because I think they form a verj essential part of the over-all role of parliamentarians ir. their review of estimates which are put before them. In the recommendations there is a real endeavour to give parliamentarians more concrete information which will enable them to do their job in committees and to make their examination of the various estimates put before them in a much more rational and meaningful method than is currently possible under the existing system.

Mr. Chairman, in the few minutes which are left I should like to ask the committee to give some thought to a matter which is of grave concern to quite a number of people in my constituency, to a large number of people on the coast of British Columbia, and to an even larger number of people who live in the Atlantic provinces. I am referring to the search and rescue service of the government.
The men who go down to the sea in ships and do business in deep waters deserve the very best kind of protection this country can provide. The men who sail our ships in the coastal trade, and the fishermen who go out to bring food back for the people of this country, are entitled to a very good, adequate, and efficient search and rescue operation. They are not getting it. The service has been both inadequate and inefficient. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich has given some of the figures, and there is no need to weary the committee with more.
The fact is that on the Pacific, coast when the herring season is on, some 1,600 fishing boats go out into deep water. Last year we lost 14 men and 13 ships, and already in this season, which has not by any means finished, we have lost four men and five ships. On the east coast there has been a steady series of losses of both ships and men.
I have in my hand the report of Mr. Justice P. Lloyd Soper, who made an inquiry into the loss of ships on the Atlantic coast and made his report to the Minister of Transport, and to the best of my knowledge not a single one of the recommendations made to that minister has been implemented.
What is the reason for the poor service which is being provided on both our coasts? I want to say that it does not lie with the men who man the coastguard or who are trying to provide the service. These men are doing the very best they can with inadequate equipment, and with a hopeless administrative structure. The main problem lies in the fact that we have divided jurisdiction. The Department of Transport, the Department of National Defence, and the Department of Fisheries are all in the picture; the RCMP also has some part in it, as has the coastguard. In addition, the United States coastguard comes to our rescue very frequently, thank heaven!

We help them, too.

On
March 18 as reported at page 11902 of Hansard I asked the Minister of National Defence about the serious losses we have suffered in the last few days both in men and boats on the Pacific coast. The minister replied:
I should point out also that maritime rescue is the responsibility of the Department of Transport. The Department of National Defence does not have a maritime rescue capability but we have a very effective air-search capability.
I asked the minister at that time how you could have a search and rescue operation in which the Department of Transport is responsible for the rescue function and the Department of National Defence is responsible for searching. That is exactly why we have had such serious losses. Moreover, we have to depend on the United States coastguard service. The minister said:
We tend to assist the U.S. more on the east coast; they assist us more on the west coast.
This may be a very good arrangement on paper but the fact remains, Mr. Chairman, when the storm hits the coastline, east or west, it hits both the American coastline and the Canadian coastline. The result is that the United States has to look after its own people. We cannot expect them to neglect servicing their people in order to meet our needs.
It seems to me this is a hopeless situation. Not only have we got a divided jurisdiction but we have inadequate equipment. The rescue operation does not have night equipment. The search operation can go out and find the ship or men clinging to a life raft, but there is no way until daybreak that the rescue operation can be effected.
What needs to be done, Mr. Chairman? I suggest the first thing is to order equipment which would make it possible to carry on both search and rescue operations 24 hours a day. We need night lights on helicopters, proper landing facilities, ships that are able to go out in stormy seas and which can fire a life line, and are strong enough to tow a stricken ship back to port.
The other thing we need is a single agency which will be responsible for the entire search and rescue operation. This divided jurisdiction has created a monstrosity. It is for the government to decide which department such an agency should come under but there certainly ought to be one agency for search and rescue, maritime and aerial, with all the facilities it needs. It should be able to go into action on both coasts. We should not have to depend on the generosity of our American friends. The men in the coastal trade or those who go out to catch fish should know that, in the event of a serious storm or running on the rocks, they have a reasonable chance of being rescued.
The other thing that needs to be (lone is for the government to accept the recommendations made by the Department of Transport, by the Department of Fisheries, and by committees of inquiry like the Soper committee and put those recommendations into effect.
The Minister of Transport was asked about this matter yesterday. As reported at page 12095 of Hansard he admitted that he had received recommendations from his department that fundamental changes were needed in the regula-

tions but these had not been made. This has been put off year after year. In the meantime brave men drown, good ships are wrecked, and ministers of the various departments pass the buck from one to the other.
The Minister of National Defence says his department is responsible for the search but the Department of Transport has to effect the rescue. The Minister of Transport told the House yesterday that these regulations are going to be promulgated later and then we will get around to doing something. Despite the fact that ministers have had the recommendations on their desks for several years nothing has been done.
It has always caused me some amusement that the Liberal party, while admitting it may not be the most innovative organization or the most imaginative in the world, has claimed to be the most competent. They believe they are the people who can be trusted to manage the affairs of Canada. But what do we see? Since the end of World War II the Liberal party has been in office for 36 out of 41 years.
Hear, hear!

Since the Tories left office the Liberal party has been in power for 13 years, eight of them in an administration headed by the present Prime Minister. Hon. members who pound their desks overlook the fact that those years will haunt them for their failure to do anything about the appalling search and rescue conditions in this country. With all those years behind them why have they not done something about this problem?
What has happened as we sit in this House has become more and more apparent. We listen to ministers say they are going to do something about the problem. They talk about appointing a task force or having a study or a report made. Then when they get the report they say the matter has to go to cabinet and that in the next six months the government will take a decision. Those are the phrases they use, Mr. Chairman.
Instead of living up to their claim as efficient administrators the government is increasingly becoming inefficient, is showing administrative incompetence. It is a bureaucracy that has grown bigger but not better, a bureaucracy that daily is becoming more insensitive to the needs of the people and less responsive to the requests of the Canadian people for action.
The President of the Treasury Board, who is a very hard working minister and a friendly person, has a duty to do more than watch the expenditures of the government. Surely he has a responsibility not just to audit the books but to audit the programs. How has it been possible that in the years he has sat on the Treasury benches nothing has been done about the divided authority and the hopelessly inefficient search and rescue operation?
For years the fishermen's union have asked for regulations which would provide for fish to be treated as cargo, so that it would be necessary to insert bulkheads in boats, to prevent fish from sliding, and ships capsizing during a storm. This was not done. They proposed to the Depart-

I say that the government has a responsibility to listen and to act on the matter. The Prime Minister has a responsibility. Perhaps it is time for him to get rid of some of the extinct volcanoes on the treasury benches and replace them with young men and women-

Mr. Chairman, I shall take only a few minutes. I thank my colleagues in the House, particularly the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, for extending this courtesy to me. I think the remarks I am about to make will reflect the thinking of the hon. member for South Shore, the hon. member for St. John's East-
The member for Halifax-East Hants.

-the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants and, indeed, all hon. members coming from the Atlantic provinces who, time and again in recent weeks, indeed in the last ten or 15 years, have spoken in this House about the inadequacy of search and rescue operations on the east coast, Gulf of St. Lawrence, on our Great Lakes and other inland waters.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands described this service as inadequate. It is. I suggest to the President of the Treasury Board that not one of the points raised this evening in connection with search and rescue involves the spending of more money. This evening we talked about the better organization and utilization of the facilities available in the Canadian Armed Forces, Department of Transport, the marine branch of the RCMP, the Department of Fisheries, our oceanographic vessels, and so on.
The Canadian government has at its disposal the fourth or fifth largest navy in the world; yet we cannot adequately protect our fishermen, including our coastal fishermen. We cannot give to coastal seamen the protection they require. I shall allude to a long list of rescue operations to make clear the magnitude of the problem. Let me make clear once more that I am not talking about the spending of more money. I am talking about the need for a better organization of existing funds and of facilities already in being and at our disposal.
The four regional search and rescue control centres last year dealt with 6,349 incidents. These search and rescue operations were co-ordinated by the four centres, in Halifax, Trenton, Edmonton, and Vancouver. Of those 6,000-odd incidents, 2,538 involved air incidents, 3,120 marine incidents, 637 were what you might call humanitarian incidents, and 55 involved aid to the civil power.
Let me say a word about the Atlantic region covering 1.8 million square miles-half the Atlantic. It runs westward to a line approximately half way down the Quebec coast, covers all the maritime provinces and goes as far north as 70 degrees north, or about 350 miles north of Frobisher Bay. Last year alone in this area we dealt with some 1,525 incidents, of which 731 were air, 619 marine and 160 were medical evacuations, or so-called humanitarian operations. We saved 210 lives. If there had been slightly more efficiency, if the available facilities had been used better, we could have saved 231 lives. That is what we are talking about. We are talking about the lives that are lost.
March 25, 1976

Two men lost their lives 150 feet from the shore of Halifax harbour because no boat or helicopter could get to them to save them. Clearly there is something desperately wrong. In Halifax harbour there are fisheries vessels, oceanographic vessels, naval vessels. These two men drowned less than a mile and a quarter away from people who might have been watching from the side of a hill. The helicopter squadron in the area could not do anything; therefore the men drowned. We mourn the loss of our seamen.
We need operational helicopters on the east coast, but at present they are not capable of operating after dark. Why, Mr. Chairman? The government will not give the Canadian military enough money to buy enough fuel so that the men flying those helicopters can maintain a night flying proficiency. They need training. You cannot send an untrained man out at night and ask him to take somebody off a pitching, foundering boat. He must be proficient. He needs training. He must be safe at what he is doing. Our personnel cannot operate safely because they have not been trained. They do not have their night flying licences. These things could be achieved without the expenditure of additional money. It involves better co-operation and utilization of existing facilities.
I shall sit down with this comment, Mr. Chairman. This will not happen in this country until there is a single, paramount authority responsible for all search and rescue. We can no longer have a divided jurisdiction. It has not saved us money. It has cost us lives. Canadians cannot afford that when we have the facilities to avoid such loss of life. I suggest that the President of the Treasury Board should consult with his colleagues in Transport, Defence, Fisheries, the coast guard, and the RCMP. They should be forced to get together and choose among them what will be the paramount authority, assuming full responsibility for all search and rescue operations in Canada. Let that single authority pull together in the most efficient way our facilities, capacities, and capabilities so that our seamen and those involved in air indicents will have the type of search and rescue operations to which they are entitled. I appreciate Your Honour's indulgence.
